newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Experts discuss Bulgarian nuclear reactor analysis.
newsitem.headline: Experts discuss Bulgarian nuclear reactor analysis.

text.p: Experts from Germany's Siemens AG and Russia's Korchatov Institute, who have analysed metal from a Bulgarian nuclear reactor, on Tuesday started talks with Bulgarian officials on their preliminary results.
Bulgaria switched off its oldest 440-megawatt reactor at Kozloduy in May for tests after the international community expressed concern over the safety of the vessel's metal.
Analysis of the samples from the Soviet-made reactor number one have been carried out by Siemens and the Korchatov Institute, which designed the plant.
Experts expect final results of the analysis, funded by the European Union's Phare programme, to be concluded in December.
Jurgen Schmidt, chief of the Siemens team which is the main contractor for the analysis, said the preliminary results "are really not bad.
"It's too early to go into more details. It is necessary to have further discussions, to further analyse these results and then come to conclusions."
Pavel Platonov, a department director at the Korchatov Institute, said the results were hopeful and would be presented to the European Commission first and then to the public.
"The only thing I can say is that the results are giving rise to optimism over the long-term fate of the reactor's vessel," Platonov said.

Stefan Vodenicharov, deputy director of the Institute of Metal Science at the Bulgarian Academy of Science, said talks between Siemens, the Korchatov Institute and Bulgarian officials in Sofia would resume on Wednesday.

"So far we were speaking about operating the (Kozloduy) reactors until the end of their lifetime but from now on we have to start working on prolonging the reactors' lifetime. And I stress: the safety prolonging of the reactors' lifetime," Vodenicharov said.
Bulgaria, which relies on the Kozloduy plant for more then 40 percent of its electricity needs, hopes to put the reactor on stream this winter in order to overcome a looming power crisis.
However, Bulgarian energy officials said that if the vessel's metal has more phosphorus than permitted, the reactor's heat removal would be inevitable.
"The problem to decide is when to carry out the heat removal, which will take several months -- this winter or next summer," said an official, who declined to be named.
